label: Cover
notes: Warden. The thesis in three words: never false-green. A green check must mean something — that the dependencies were actually assessed and found safe. Warden is a CI gate for BOTH Python ecosystems: pip/PyPI apps and the conda/conda-forge scientific and ML/AI world.

label: Act I
notes: Act I frames the problem. A CI gate's whole job is to answer one question honestly: is this safe to merge? The danger isn't a red X — it's a green check that never actually looked.

label: Exit 0 ≠ safe
notes: Every CI gate reduces to an exit code. 0 merges, non-zero blocks. But exit 0 conflates two very different states: 'I checked and it's clean' and 'I didn't really check.' A scanner that finds nothing returns 0 whether it looked hard or not at all.

label: False-green: empty DB
notes: First false-green mode: the empty or corrupt vulnerability database. If the OSV database failed to download, is empty, or is stale, a naive scanner queries it, gets zero hits, and reports clean. You get a green check that means the opposite of safe.

label: False-green: unassessable
notes: Second false-green mode: the unassessable dependency. deptry and osv-scanner don't parse conda meta.yaml, recipe.yaml, environment.yml, or pixi.toml. A naive pipeline silently skips what it can't read — so a conda-heavy ML repo scans 'clean' while most of its dependencies were never seen.

label: Two ecosystems
notes: The blind spot has structure. Python is really two ecosystems: PyPI — 850K packages, open upload, any license — and conda-forge — 30K curated, FOSS-only feedstocks. Applications are 20% of the enterprise footprint; the ML/AI/data stack is a tiny slice of apps but 80% of the distinct libraries. Warden covers both.

label: Act II
notes: Act II: the contract. Warden's answer to false-green is a single, frozen, machine-readable contract — one report schema, one verdict lattice, one exit enum. Nothing downstream has to guess.

label: One report
notes: Everything flows into one artifact: the ComplianceReport, validated against a committed JSON Schema. Both engines, all axes, coverage, and provenance merge here. It's producer-agnostic and the single source of truth — the human summary is just a rendering of it.

label: Verdict lattice
notes: The verdict lattice — seven rungs, highest wins. error and policy-violation and indeterminate all block; warn, bypassed, clean, not-applicable all pass. The key design move: indeterminate sits ABOVE the pass line. An unproven result blocks, it never slides to clean.

label: Exit enum
notes: The exit enum is frozen: 0 success, 1 policy violation or indeterminate, 2 operational error, 130 interrupted. Four values, no drift. CI wires against these forever. And every operational failure is a typed error with a named owner — unparsable-manifest, engine-unavailable, engine-crash, internal-error — so a failure routes to whoever can fix it.

label: Act III
notes: Act III: the engines and how they run. Warden orchestrates deptry and osv-scanner behind one report, reads six manifest formats natively, isolates each engine behind a hardened subprocess seam, and scans at three concentric rings of the supply chain.

label: deptry — hygiene
notes: Axis 1, hygiene, ships in v1 with deptry. It does AST import analysis and cross-checks against declared dependencies, emitting DEP001 through DEP005: missing, unused, transitive, misplaced-dev, and duplicate. It honors existing tool.deptry ignore config so teams keep their tuning.

label: osv-scanner — security
notes: Axis 2, security, ships in v1 with Google's osv-scanner checked against the OSV database. Crucially the database is provisioned as a declared conda/pixi dependency — never a runtime curl — and Warden pre-flights it for freshness and integrity before trusting a result. That's the fix for false-green #1.

label: Subprocess seam
notes: The engines are external binaries, so Warden isolates each behind a hardened subprocess seam: no shell, explicit argv, timeouts and resource caps, captured stdout/stderr, and a distinction between an engine that's unavailable versus one that crashed. A misbehaving engine becomes a typed error and exit 2 — never a silent pass.

label: Six manifests
notes: The manifest engine is the wedge: neither stock engine parses conda or pixi. Warden reads all six formats — pyproject.toml and pixi.toml via tomllib, requirements.txt by line-parse, environment.yml, meta.yaml v0 with jinja/selector neutralization, and recipe.yaml v1 — all via yaml.safe_load. No untrusted input is ever executed.

label: Three rings
notes: Warden runs at three depths, and the further out it scans, the more it prevents rather than reports. Consumption edge — repos, desktops, CI — is today. Registry perimeter — block/allow lists on Artifactory/JFrog — is v1.x and the star: a census of everything that enters. Public upstream — scanning PyPI and conda-forge for malicious and typosquat packages — is the vision.

label: Act IV
notes: Act IV: offline and air-gap trust. Enterprise Python often runs where the internet doesn't reach. Warden is built for that: deny-by-default egress, deterministic runs, and a database it verifies before it trusts.

label: Deny-by-default egress
notes: Warden makes no network calls during a scan by default. The database and engines are provisioned ahead of time as declared dependencies. Any online behavior is opt-in and explicit, never silent. That's what makes runs safe in regulated and air-gapped environments.

label: Deterministic runs
notes: Two properties make Warden auditable. Determinism: pinned engines and a pinned database mean the same inputs give the same verdict, every time, on any machine. And the pre-flight: Warden verifies the database's record count, freshness, and integrity before trusting it. Together these turn a scan into evidence you can defend in an audit.

label: First contact
notes: Adoption starts at a terminal, not a pipeline. warden scan . --warn-only runs locally, shows real findings, and exits 0 so nobody is blocked on day one. This is the on-ramp — see it work on your own machine before you ever touch CI.

label: Act V
notes: Act V: from a gate to a governance platform. The same contract extends across six axes of dependency trust — and the engines are pluggable, so new signals slot in behind the same report and the same lattice.

label: Six axes
notes: Six axes, each a different question. Hygiene: is it used? Security: is it vulnerable? These ship in v1. License: is it allowed? Currency: is it patchable / supported? These complete the v1.x gate. Provenance: is it authentic? Maintenance: is it maintained? These are the vision. All behind one report, one lattice.

label: KEV / EPSS
notes: v1.x enriches the security axis to prioritize by real-world exploitability. Not every CVE matters equally. CISA KEV tells you it's being exploited in the wild right now. FIRST EPSS gives a probability it will be. Together they let the gate block on what's actually dangerous — critical, KEV-listed, or high-EPSS — instead of drowning teams in theoretical findings.

label: License & currency
notes: Two more axes complete the v1.x gate. License: read SPDX expressions from PyPI metadata and conda recipe about-license via license-expression, and gate on allow/deny lists — an unreadable license is indeterminate, not clean. Currency: use endoflife.date plus version-lag to flag EOL and out-of-date dependencies, and the Python runtime itself against LTS / N / N-1. Only current things get patched.

label: Act VI
notes: Act VI: the payoff. Everything reduces to one command with one trustworthy exit code. Wire it into CI and the same honest verdict runs fleet-wide.

label: Gate in CI
notes: Here's the same command as a CI check. It blocks the merge with exit 1 on a KEV-listed critical, and the check surfaces the exact finding and the report artifact. Green is earned — by locking, waiving with an expiring reason, or fixing — never faked.

label: Never false-green
notes: The close. A bare recipe.yaml scan exits non-zero by design until you lock, waive, or run warn-only. That's the lock-nudge working, not a bug. Warden's promise is simple: a green check means it was actually checked.

label: Appendix · Personas
notes: Appendix: who Warden serves at the executive level. The CISO gets exploitability-prioritized risk and audit evidence. The Chief Developer Experience Officer gets a gate that runs locally first and doesn't cry wolf. The CIO gets fleet-wide standardization and offline compliance. The Chief Data & Analytics Officer gets coverage of the conda/ML footprint that stock tools miss.
